Human Immunodeficiency Virus — 2026 · Microbiology & Antiretroviral Pharmacology

HIV: Structure, Replication & Antiretroviral Therapy

The virus infects primarily CD4 T-cells. Early in infection viral Ribonucleic Acid (RNA) is reverse transcribed to form double-stranded Deoxyribonucleic Acid (DNA), which integrates into the host cell chromosome — establishing a persistent infection that damages the immune system and predisposes to opportunistic infections and malignancies.

Virion Size100–150 nm
Structural GenesPol · Gag · Env
Replication Steps5 (+ ART class each)
AIDS ThresholdCD4 < 200/µL (<14%)
Latency Period~10 years
Orientation

How to hold this lecture

Overview: One Idea, Then Everything Else

🔑 The Central Sequence

HIV infects CD4 T-cells → viral RNA is reverse transcribed into double-stranded DNA → that DNA integrates into the host chromosome (provirus) → the infection becomes persistent and latent → the immune system is progressively damaged → opportunistic infections and malignancies follow. Every section of this outline is an elaboration of one link in that chain, and every antiretroviral drug class is named for the step it blocks.

Why HIV Is So Hard to Eradicate — Three Advantages

1

Genetic diversity

Highly mutable. Reverse transcriptase has a high error rate, which is the direct source of drug-resistance mutations.

2

Latency

Integrated provirus can sit transcriptionally silent, invisible to drugs that only target actively replicating virus.

3

Attacks the immune response itself

Targets CD4 T-cells and macrophages — the very cells that would clear it.

🧬 Why "Retrovirus"

The designation refers to the use of reverse transcriptase to form a double-stranded DNA intermediate called the provirus — reversing the usual DNA → RNA direction of information flow. Baltimore Group VI (single-stranded RNA with reverse transcriptase).

Section A — HIV Structure & Function

Virology

Structure, Genes, and Gene Products

  • 100–150 nm, outer envelope containing 2 glycoprotein spikes (gp120, gp41) and 2 copies of single-stranded RNA.
  • Major structural genes: Pol, Gag, Env.

Slide 3 — HIV virion structure (Baltimore Group VI, single-stranded RNA with reverse transcriptase)

Pol Gene (Polymerase) Products — The Three Enzymes

EnzymeFunctionExam hook
Reverse transcriptase (RT)RNA-dependent DNA polymerase — synthesizes the HIV provirusHigh error rate → the source of HIV diversity and of resistance
Integrase (IN)Integrates provirus DNA into the host genomeThe irreversible step; target of the INSTI class
Protease (aspartyl protease)Cleaves the precursor protein products of the pol and gag genesWithout it, virions are immature and non-infectious

Gag Gene (Group-Specific Antigen) Products

A p55 precursor (55 kDa) is cleaved by viral protease into the structural proteins:

ProductRoleNote
p24Capsid core antigenEasiest to detect in sera — this is the p24 antigen used in 4th-generation testing. Also has a role in bringing the pre-integration complex (PIC) into the host chromosome
p17Matrix proteinLines the inner envelope
p6 / p7 / p9Nucleocapsid proteinsBind the viral RNA genome

Env Gene (Envelope) Products

A 160 kDa precursor cleaved by host protease (contrast: gag/pol precursors are cleaved by viral protease) into:

🔑

gp120 — the binding protein

Binds to target cells: the CD4 receptor plus a chemokine co-receptor, CCR5 or CXCR4.

🔗

gp41 — the fusion protein

Contains the "fusogenic domain" that enables fusion with the host cell membrane.

Regulatory and Accessory Genes

Starred genes are of increased interest for ART development.

GeneFunction
tat*Activator of transcription — also inhibits T-cell proliferation
revRegulates viral expression — enhances expression
vifVirion infectivity
vpr*Viral protein R — nuclear incorporation of the PIC, enhances replication, arrests host cell cycle progression
vpuViral protein U — enhances viral release from host; downregulates CD4 surface expression, interfering with complexes that inhibit viral production
nef*Negative regulatory function — protects HIV-infected cells from killing by T lymphocytes

Q: Which HIV protein is the easiest to detect in serum, and which gene encodes it?

Answer

p24, the capsid protein, encoded by the gag gene. It is cleaved from the p55 precursor by viral protease.

This is why p24 antigen is paired with antibody detection in the combination immunoassay — it becomes detectable before antibodies do, which is what lets 4th-generation testing catch acute infection.

Section B — Replication Cycle, ART Targets & Resistance

The core of the lecture

Five Steps, Their Drug Classes, and How Resistance Defeats Each

This is the section the outline develops in the most depth: for each replication step, the related antiretroviral (ART) class, an example drug, and the specific resistance mechanism. Learn it as a five-row table and the pharmacology becomes recall rather than memorization.

Slides 19 / 23 / 31 / 34 — The HIV replication cycle

Slides 20 / 25 / 32 / 35 — Each drug class mapped to the step it blocks

Step 1 — Attachment / Fusion

gp120 binds the CD4 receptor or the CCR5 / CXCR4 chemokine receptor → initiates a conformational change in the envelope, exposing gp41, which fuses with the membrane → cell entry.

Fostemsavir

Attachment inhibitor — binds gp120

Impedes gp120 binding to CD4/CCR5/CXCR4.

Maraviroc

CCR5 antagonist — binds CCR5/CXCR4

Prevents virus binding to CCR5 of the helper T-cell.

Enfuvirtide

Fusion inhibitor — binds gp41

Prevents fusion of gp41 with the host membrane.

Ibalizumab

Post-attachment entry inhibitor — monoclonal antibody

Blocks CD4 receptors on other immune cells — virus can attach but can't enter.

⚠️ Resistance at Step 1
  • Fostemsavir: a high rate of gp120 amino acid substitutions reduces the drug's binding efficiency.
  • Maraviroc: amino acid substitution in gp120 that facilitates binding to the drug-altered conformation of the receptor.
  • Enfuvirtide: amino acid substitution in viral gp41 → no binding of drug.

Step 2 — Uncoating and Genome Release

Viral genome is released within the host. Capsid material remains and helps chaperone the pre-integration complex (PIC) into the nucleus — this is why the capsid is itself a drug target.

Step 3 — Reverse Transcription

Synthesis of complementary double-stranded DNA (cDNA / provirus) via reverse transcriptase. The reverse transcription complex (RTC) — matrix protein, capsid protein, integrase, reverse transcriptase and viral protein R — transitions into the pre-integration complex (PIC), which is transported to the nucleus.

🧩

NRTI — Nucleoside RT Inhibitors

Competitive binding to reverse transcriptase → cDNA chain termination. Often used in pairs.

  • Azidothymidine (AZT, zidovudine) — thymidine analogue
  • Tenofovir — adenosine analogue

Resistance: viral RT point mutations reduce affinity of NRTI binding.

🔒

NNRTI — Non-Nucleoside (Allosteric) RT Inhibitors

Non-competitive inhibition — cause conformational changes in reverse transcriptase.

  • Efavirenz
  • Doravirine

Resistance: a single point mutation on conserved RT domains can inactivate all class members — a much lower genetic barrier than NRTIs.

Slide 29 — NNRTI mechanism: the inhibitor binds reverse transcriptase and denatures it, so the enzyme cannot produce viral DNA

Capsid Inhibitors — Lenacapavir

Disrupts the capsid after uncoating → obstructs PIC transport to the nucleus. It also acts later in the cycle (see Step 5), which is what makes it a multi-stage agent.

Resistance: a mutation in the HIV-1 capsid confers > 80,000-fold resistance to lenacapavir.

Step 4 — Provirus Integration

Integration into the host genome via integrase.

Raltegravir

INSTI — integrase strand transfer inhibitor

Prevents strand transfer of viral DNA into the host genome.

Cabotegravir

INSTI — also available long-acting injectable

Used for treatment and, as Apretude®, for pre-exposure prophylaxis.

Resistance: mutations that alter integrase structure → decreased drug binding.

Step 5 — Synthesis, Assembly, Maturation, Release

  • Assembly near the host cell surface
  • Budding
  • Cleavage (via protease) of the precursor gag/pol proteins → p6, p7, p17, p24; RT, IN

Atazanavir

Protease inhibitor

Prevents maturation by inhibiting cleavage of gag and gag/pol precursors.

Darunavir

Protease inhibitor

Same mechanism; virions remain immature and non-infectious.

Lenacapavir

Capsid inhibitor (late-stage action)

Disrupts capsid entry into the host nucleus and assembly of new progeny capsid — new virions cannot replicate in a new host.

🩺 Resistance Contrast Worth Memorizing

Protease inhibitors: resistance is uncommon unless the patient was previously treated with a protease inhibitor — a notably high genetic barrier. Compare with NNRTIs, where a single point mutation can knock out the entire class. Lenacapavir sits at the other extreme: one capsid mutation confers a > 80,000-fold shift.

Step 6 — Pharmacokinetic Enhancers

Cobicistat (Tybost®)

Not an antiretroviral itself — it interferes with the in vivo metabolic breakdown of antiretroviral drugs, raising their levels. ("Slows metabolic breakdown of the anti-HIV drug.")

Step 7 — Pre-Exposure Prophylaxis (PrEP)

Recommended for uninfected individuals at high risk for exposure to HIV.

ProductAgent(s)Route
Truvada®Emtricitabine / tenofovirOral
Descovy®Emtricitabine / tenofovir alafenamideOral
Apretude®CabotegravirIntramuscular injection
Yeztugo®LenacapavirInjection and oral

Step 8 — Post-Exposure Prophylaxis (PEP)

🔑 PEP

Given following occupational exposure to HIV (blood / body fluids). Example: triple therapy — tenofovir + emtricitabine with raltegravir.

Step 9 — In the Pipeline

  • RNA nanomedicines — reduce expression of the CCR5 target by host cells, or expression of viral nef in infected cells.
  • mRNA and other vaccines — on hold.

General Mechanisms of Resistance

🧬 Mutations in the Virus Target Site

Amino acid alterations modify the structural conformation of HIV enzymes (reverse transcriptase, protease, integrase), decreasing drug binding. The upstream cause is always the same: reverse transcriptase's high error rate generates the variant pool that selection then acts on.

Q: A patient's virus develops a single point mutation in a conserved domain of reverse transcriptase. Which drug class is most likely to be rendered entirely ineffective, and why does the other reverse-transcriptase class fare better?

Answer

The NNRTIs (efavirenz, doravirine). A single point mutation on a conserved RT domain can inactivate all members of the class, because they all bind the same allosteric pocket non-competitively.

NRTIs (AZT, tenofovir) fare better because their resistance mechanism is different — point mutations reduce the affinity of NRTI binding rather than abolishing it, and NRTIs bind competitively at the active site as nucleoside analogues, so they generally require accumulated mutations rather than one.

Q: Match each agent to its replication step — fostemsavir, raltegravir, darunavir, enfuvirtide, doravirine, lenacapavir, cobicistat.

Answer
  • Fostemsavir — Step 1, attachment (binds gp120)
  • Enfuvirtide — Step 1, fusion (binds gp41)
  • Doravirine — Step 3, reverse transcription (NNRTI, allosteric)
  • Lenacapavir — Steps 2/3 and 5, capsid (blocks PIC transport; disrupts progeny capsid assembly)
  • Raltegravir — Step 4, integration (INSTI)
  • Darunavir — Step 5, maturation (protease inhibitor)
  • Cobicistat — none of them; it is a pharmacokinetic enhancer, not an antiretroviral
Section C — Transmission

Epidemiology

Transmission

  • Can establish latency.
  • Common modes: sexual; exposure to contaminated body fluids; vertical transmission (mother → infant); occupational exposure; sharing contaminated needles.
  • Agent is easily inactivated outside of the host.
  • Primarily spread in blood, semen, and cervical secretions.
  • No insect vectors identified.
  • Primary target: helper T-cells and monocytes.
⚠️ Two Facts That Get Tested as Negatives

"No insect vectors" and "easily inactivated outside the host" are both frequently examined — they rule out fomite and vector transmission, which distinguishes HIV from many other infectious agents on a differential.

Section D — Pathophysiology & Clinical Stages

Natural history

Pathophysiology and the Three Stages

Pathophysiology of Infection

  1. Early From the original infective site (T-cells), infection is established in lymphoid tissue and the central nervous system. High transmission likelihood in this window.
  2. Weeks later HIV-specific T-cells appear in blood → destruction of CD4 cells. The patient is asymptomatic, or manifests non-specific symptoms.
  3. Late (> several months) Increasing virus with decreasing CD4 cells — the patient is still asymptomatic. Typical symptom-free period: 10 years.
🔑 Threshold to Memorize

Risk of opportunistic infection is greatest when CD4 < 50/µL. (Contrast with the definition of AIDS at CD4 < 200/µL — the definitional threshold and the maximum-risk threshold are different numbers.)

Slide 41 — HIV progression: CD4 cells fall as virus rises, over weeks-to-months then years

The Three Stages

StageTimingCD4 countCD4 %Opportunistic infections
Acute (Stage 1, pre-AIDS)2–4 weeks post-infection≥ 500/µL≥ 29%None
Chronic (clinical latency)Many years (~10)FallingFallingNone — few symptoms
AIDS (Stage 3)~3 years' survival without treatment< 200/µL< 14%Onset of opportunistic infections

Typical Presentations — Stage 3 (AIDS)

Slide 43 — Typical symptoms in stage 3

  • Weight loss · chronic diarrhea · night sweats · fever · persistent cough
  • Mouth and skin problems · regular infections
  • Malignancies — Kaposi sarcoma, B-cell lymphoma
Section E — Diagnosis

Laboratory

Diagnostic Assays

✅

Serologic (ELISA) — Recommended

  • Combined anti-HIV-1/HIV-2 antibody and HIV p24 antigen detection
  • Confirmatory: HIV-1/HIV-2 antibody differentiation immunoassay
🧪

Non-Serologic — Not required for diagnosis

  • HIV RNA — qualitative nucleic acid amplification
  • Quantitative PCR — primarily used for monitoring viral load during treatment, not for making the diagnosis

Slide 46 — Recommended laboratory HIV diagnostic testing algorithm

  1. HIV-1/2 antigen/antibody combination immunoassay Negative for HIV-1 and HIV-2 antibodies and p24 antigen → HIV negative.
  2. If reactive → HIV-1/HIV-2 antibody differentiation immunoassay Resolves to HIV-1 positive, HIV-2 positive, HIV positive untypable, or indeterminate/negative.
  3. If indeterminate or negative on differentiation → nucleic acid test (NAT) A positive NAT here indicates acute HIV-1 infection — antibodies have not yet developed.

Slide 45 — Rapid point-of-care HIV-1/2 test (10–20 minutes)

Q: A patient's combination antigen/antibody immunoassay is reactive, but the HIV-1/HIV-2 antibody differentiation immunoassay is indeterminate. What is the next step, and what would a positive result mean?

Answer

Perform a nucleic acid test (NAT). A positive NAT in this setting indicates acute HIV-1 infection.

The logic: the combination assay picked up p24 antigen (which appears early), while antibodies — which the differentiation assay looks for — have not yet developed. That gap between antigen and antibody is exactly what the third tier resolves.

Section F — Opportunistic Infections & Malignancies

Consequences of immune failure

Common Opportunistic Infections in HIV-AIDS

🔑 Three Tiers to Sort Them By
  • Most common organisms: Toxoplasma gondii, Pneumocystis jiroveci, Candida species, Cryptococcus neoformans, M. tuberculosis, Mycobacterium avium-intracellulare complex, herpes simplex viruses 1 and 2, varicella-zoster virus (VZV), and cytomegalovirus (CMV).
  • Less common — within specific exposure or geographic contexts: Leishmania, Trypanosoma cruzi, Bartonella, Listeria monocytogenes, Histoplasma capsulatum, Coccidioides, Cryptosporidium.
  • Neoplastic / preneoplastic: Kaposi sarcoma (HHV-8), lymphomas (EBV), HPV-associated lesions, and demyelinating disease — progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy (PML) caused by JC virus.

Q: Name the viral agent behind each of these AIDS-associated conditions: Kaposi sarcoma, primary central nervous system / B-cell lymphoma, progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy, and cervical or anal squamous cell carcinoma.

Answer
  • Kaposi sarcoma → HHV-8 (human herpesvirus 8)
  • B-cell lymphoma (Hodgkin / non-Hodgkin) → EBV (HHV-4)
  • Progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy → JC virus (a polyomavirus)
  • Cervical / anal / oral squamous cell carcinoma → HPV, types 16 and 18

All four are examples of the outline's third tier — neoplastic or preneoplastic conditions, driven by oncogenic viruses that an intact immune system would normally hold in check.

🎯 HIV 2026 — High-Yield One-Pager

By outline section — A structure · B cycle & ART · C transmission · D stages · E diagnosis · F opportunistic infections

A · STRUCTURE & GENES

Virion

  • 100–150 nm; envelope with 2 glycoprotein spikes (gp120, gp41); 2 copies ssRNA
  • "Retrovirus" = uses reverse transcriptase → dsDNA intermediate (provirus)
  • Advantages: genetic diversity (highly mutable) · latency · attacks immune cells (CD4 T-cells, macrophages)

Pol → the 3 enzymes

  • Reverse transcriptase — RNA-dependent DNA polymerase; high error rate → HIV diversity + resistance
  • Integrase — provirus into host genome
  • Protease (aspartyl) — cleaves pol/gag precursors

Gag → p55 precursor, cleaved by VIRAL protease

  • p24 — capsid; EASIEST TO DETECT IN SERA; role in PIC entry to host chromosome
  • p17 — matrix · p6/p7/p9 — nucleocapsid

Env → 160 kDa, cleaved by HOST protease

  • gp120 — binds CD4, CCR5, CXCR4
  • gp41 — "fusogenic domain," fuses with membrane

Regulatory / accessory (* = ART interest)

  • tat* — activates transcription; inhibits T-cell proliferation
  • rev — enhances expression · vif — virion infectivity
  • vpr* — nuclear PIC incorporation; arrests host cell cycle
  • vpu — enhances release; downregulates CD4 surface expression
  • nef* — protects infected cells from T-lymphocyte killing
B · CYCLE → DRUG → RESISTANCE

1. Attachment / Fusion

  • Fostemsavir (binds gp120) — R: high rate of gp120 aa substitutions ↓ binding
  • Maraviroc (CCR5/CXCR4) — R: gp120 aa substitution allows binding to drug-altered conformation
  • Enfuvirtide (binds gp41) — R: aa substitution in gp41, no drug binding
  • Ibalizumab — post-attachment entry inhibitor, monoclonal Ab; virus attaches but can't enter

2. Uncoating

  • Capsid remains, chaperones PIC into nucleus

3. Reverse transcription (RTC → PIC → nucleus)

  • NRTI — competitive, chain termination; AZT (thymidine analogue), tenofovir (adenosine analogue). R: RT point mutations ↓ affinity
  • NNRTI — non-competitive/allosteric, conformational change; efavirenz, doravirine. R: SINGLE point mutation on conserved RT domain inactivates ALL class members
  • Capsid inhibitor — lenacapavir: obstructs PIC transport. R: capsid mutation = >80,000-fold resistance

4. Integration

  • INSTI — raltegravir, cabotegravir. R: mutations alter integrase structure → ↓ drug binding

5. Assembly / budding / maturation

  • Protease inhibitors — atazanavir, darunavir. R: UNCOMMON unless previously PI-treated
  • Lenacapavir also acts here — progeny cannot replicate in a new host

6–9. Adjuncts & prophylaxis

  • Cobicistat (Tybost®) — pharmacokinetic enhancer, slows metabolic breakdown (NOT an antiretroviral)
  • PrEP: Truvada®/Descovy® (emtricitabine + tenofovir, oral) · Apretude® (cabotegravir, IM) · Yeztugo® (lenacapavir)
  • PEP: occupational exposure → tenofovir-emtricitabine + raltegravir
  • Pipeline: RNA nanomedicines (↓ CCR5 or nef); mRNA vaccines on hold

General resistance mechanism

  • aa alterations change structural conformation of RT / protease / integrase → ↓ drug binding
C · TRANSMISSION

Modes & facts

  • Sexual · contaminated body fluids · vertical (mother → infant) · occupational · shared needles
  • Spread primarily in blood, semen, cervical secretions
  • Easily inactivated outside the host
  • NO insect vectors
  • Primary target: helper T-cells, monocytes
D · PATHOPHYS & STAGES

Course

  • Early: infection established in lymphoid tissue + CNS; high transmission likelihood
  • Weeks later: HIV-specific T-cells appear → CD4 destruction; asymptomatic or non-specific
  • Late (>months): ↑ virus, ↓ CD4, still asymptomatic
  • Symptom-free period ≈ 10 years
  • OI risk greatest when CD4 < 50/µL

Three stages — numbers

  • Acute (2–4 wk): CD4 ≥ 500/µL, ≥ 29%, no OI
  • Chronic: asymptomatic latency, few symptoms, no OI
  • AIDS: CD4 < 200/µL, < 14%, onset of OI, ~3 yr survival untreated

Stage 1 symptoms (%)

  • Fever 80 · fatigue 78 · malaise 68 · arthralgia 54 · headache 54 · anorexia 54 · rash 51 · night sweats 51
  • Also pharyngitis, lymphadenopathy, myalgia

Stage 3 presentations

  • Weight loss, chronic diarrhea, night sweats, fever, persistent cough, mouth/skin problems, recurrent infections, malignancies (Kaposi, B-cell lymphoma)
E · DIAGNOSIS

Serologic (ELISA) — recommended

  • Combined anti-HIV-1/2 antibody + p24 antigen
  • Confirmatory: HIV-1/HIV-2 antibody differentiation immunoassay

Non-serologic — NOT required for diagnosis

  • HIV RNA — qualitative nucleic acid amplification
  • Quantitative PCR — monitoring viral load during treatment

Algorithm

  • Ag/Ab combination immunoassay → if (−) for both antibodies and p24, HIV negative
  • If (+) → antibody differentiation → HIV-1 pos / HIV-2 pos / untypable / indeterminate
  • Indeterminate or (−) → NAT; positive = acute HIV-1 infection
F · OPPORTUNISTIC INFECTIONS

Most common organisms

  • Toxoplasma gondii, Pneumocystis jiroveci, Candida, Cryptococcus neoformans, M. tuberculosis, MAC, HSV 1/2, VZV, CMV

Virus → tumor pairings (very testable)

  • HHV-8 → Kaposi sarcoma
  • EBV (HHV-4) → B-cell lymphoma (Hodgkin/non-Hodgkin)
  • HPV 16, 18 → cervical/anal/oral squamous cell carcinoma
  • JC virus → PML (demyelinating)
  • CMV (HHV-5) → retinitis, pneumonia, GI, encephalitis

Reactivation vs primary

  • Reactivation: TB (pulmonary + disseminated), HSV 1/2 (oral/genital/anal, pneumonitis, esophagitis), VZV → shingles
  • Fungi: Candida albicans (thrush = pseudomembranous; esophagitis), Pneumocystis jirovecii (pneumonia), Cryptococcus neoformans (pneumonia, meningoencephalitis)
  • Protozoa: Cryptosporidium, Cystoisospora belli (diarrhea); Toxoplasma (encephalitis)
  • Bacteria: MAC, M. kansasii (extrapulmonary), Bartonella henselae (bacillary angiomatosis), Salmonella enterica (recurrent septicemia), S. pneumoniae (recurrent pneumonia)

Histology hook

  • Herpetic esophagitis → multinucleated giant cells
